title: Agent Authorization Explained
summary: Authorization is several checks in sequence, not one. The intersection rule, where OAuth scopes stop being enough, how RFC 8693 carries two identities, and the failures that look identical.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Authorization is not one decision. It's several, checked in sequence, and most agent incidents trace back to only one of them ever being checked.** A team wires up a login, confirms the agent is who it says it is, and calls that "authorized", but identity only answers who is acting, not what they're allowed to do.


The standards already assume the gap. OAuth 2.1 says plainly that "access tokens are intended to be issued to clients with less privileges than the user granting the access has." AWS builds the same idea into IAM, where a session's permissions are "the intersection of the identity-based policies for the IAM entity" and the session policy.


The common shortcut treats authentication as a stand-in for authorization: verify the agent, assume the rest is fine. A perfectly identified agent with no limit on its reach is exactly as dangerous as an anonymous one, because identity tells you who broke something, not whether they were allowed to.


None of this means locking agents down until they're useless. The opposite failure is just as common and harder to notice: an agent that quietly inherits everything the person it serves can do, looking fine right up until the day it uses that inherited reach.


What holds up is layered. A request clears identity, then who it's acting for, then which tool, then which action, then which data, before it runs at all. Design the layers before you design the login screen.
